prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis on clustered templates

statement.case_for: Massively parallel sequencing is a game-changer in the sense I apply: a completely new capability whose consequences are already demonstrated at scale. Sequencing cost fell by orders of magnitude, and genomics, clinical diagnostics, cancer and infectious-disease monitoring and much of modern biomolecular science now depend on it. The core is chemistry: reversible-terminator nucleotides, fluorescent labelling, surface-bound clonal amplification and single-molecule detection. Four members ranked it in their top two, three of them first, and the technology has been in universal use for about twenty years, so recognition is overdue rather than premature. Four members already propose the Balasubramanian-Klenerman core, and the question is whether the third seat goes to Mayer.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. Three seats cannot cover Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Mayer, Ju and Rothberg, and the pyrosequencing/454 lineage is a distinct route that would be left out entirely. Sanger sequencing was honoured in 1980, so some will read this as a scale-up of a recognised method rather than a new principle. If the committee cannot agree on a defensible third name, the cleaner option is the Cambridge pair alone, and a fallback to B048 would then be justified on cleanliness of attribution.

responses.point: Daniel ranks B017 first but proposes only Balasubramanian and Klenerman, arguing a two-person award is cleanest even though it excludes real contributors.
responses.response: I agree the Cambridge pair is the core, but I would still include Mayer. The clonal clustering concept, colonies on a surface from single molecules, is what made the chemistry scale, and leaving it out makes the citation about the nucleotide chemistry only. I accept this is a judgment call about the third seat and not a point of principle, and I would not block a two-person award if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Andrei also ranks B017 first with the Cambridge pair, noting Mayer, Ju and Rothberg are credited and that he is unsure of the decisive split.
responses.response: I share the uncertainty, but Rothberg's pyrosequencing and semiconductor route and Ju's terminator chemistry are different technical lines that did not become the dominant platform chemistry. The prize should reward the line that carried the field. I would welcome any argument from Andrei, who knows nucleotide enzymology better than I do, on whether Ju's terminator work was truly independent or ancillary.

responses.point: Peter ranks Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling first, calling it mature, general and complementary to the 2010 cross-coupling prize and not redundant.
responses.response: This is my second choice and I agree on attribution: Buchwald and Hartwig are a clean pair, and Kosugi's tin-amide precedent was not the general catalytic method. My reservation is only that the 2010 prize makes several members hesitate, and Peter is better placed than I am to say whether the ligand-design advance is conceptually distinct. I rank it second, not first, because sequencing's change to the field is of greater scale.

responses.point: Heiner, as chair, ranks perovskite solar absorbers first for a clear physical principle plus new capability, with sequencing second.
responses.response: I put perovskites eighth and keep that view. The efficiency story is remarkable, but stability and commercial viability are unproven, and the credit among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel, Kanatzidis and Seok is crowded. A prize should reward what has already shown lasting consequences. I do agree with Heiner that B017 belongs at the top of the list, and our shared three-name proposal with Mayer suggests we can converge there.

responses.point: Peter B. ranks nitrogenase first, as a physical-chemical account of multi-electron proton-coupled catalysis unifying genetics, crystallography and kinetics.
responses.response: Nitrogenase is scientifically deep and I respect the case, but the catalytic mechanism is still debated, so the final story is incomplete, and a prize for structure alone would leave out the part that matters most. The three-seat split among Rees, Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe is also hard. I remain unpersuaded for this year but would want to hear whether he sees mechanism as settled enough.

uncertainties: Whether Mayer's clustering contribution is decisive enough to take the third seat over Ju or Rothberg.
Whether the committee would treat sequencing by synthesis as a new principle or an extension of Sanger sequencing.
Whether the 2010 cross-coupling prize weighs against B048 for the committee, which affects my fallback.
Priority claims among the sequencing groups rest on my background knowledge and are not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Warshel/EVB and Uppsala biomolecular simulation background is related to B037 (protein folding theory), but I have no personal or institutional tie to its candidates and do not support it.
